cards.tip: WIN — When the customer mentioned 'I'm home today,' Francisco responded with 'I'll take a look at this and then give you a full report'—his immediate offer combined with 24/7 availability messaging converted the Costco lead into an active inspection visit.

WIN — Andrew reconnected the customer's expired Sunrise maintenance plan to a $16/month offer that saves money versus one-time service, turning discovery into an immediate upsell by solving an existing need.

WIN — When the customer expressed worry about investing in a motor repair on an aging system, Andrew empathized with that concern and pivoted to Option C (Comfort Advisor replacement consultation), which earned the scheduled appointment.
FIX — No job number means this was likely a dispatch error or false alarm—clarify the appointment upfront before arriving to avoid wasted time.

FIX — You presented clear options (repair vs. upgrade), but when the customer hesitated, you didn't ask a reconnecting question—try 'Which concern matters more: the upfront cost or getting a longer-term fix?'

WIN — When the customer expressed distrust about the membership being intrusive and pushy, you validated their concern and immediately offered an alternative path forward with tune-up promotions instead. That empathy-first approach converted their resistance into an agreement for the $366 repair.

FIX — You discovered the AC unit running 13-20 hrs/day and filter maintenance need, but didn't present an upgrade or next-step option when the customer mentioned potential power concerns—create the follow-up: 'Given the high runtime, we should have our specialist look at efficiency options.'

FIX — Capacitor repair closed but equipment specialist appointment wasn't scheduled (customer said they'd call after court). Lock in a specific time for specialist visit before leaving the house to convert repeat customer into equipment sale flip.
WIN — Excellent technical education on compressor failure root cause earned the equipment specialist appointment by building trust through explaining non-condensables from poor installation.

WIN — She couldn't decide between $10k repairs and replacement; you said "If he comes out, that doesn't mean you have to get the system—it's just so you get the information," and offered 8 AM tomorrow; she booked because you removed the pressure.

FIX — When you found the hot fan motor, you should've told the customer: 'The motor's running hot, which means your system isn't getting proper airflow—that's why you're getting hot air. I'm heading to the attic coil now,' instead of just heading off to grab tools without explaining your findings.

FIX — Strong assessment and options presentation undermined by lack of clear close; customer never commits to specific repair path before tech leaves, creating follow-up work and lost urgency; use trial close during decision stage to confirm option preference before concluding visit.
FIX — System age and maintenance observations provide entry points for Option C consultation; present a Comfort Advisor visit when equipment age or system issues surface during discovery.

FIX — Your rapport is excellent, but after the evaluation, always frame when you're coming back with options and make it a committed appointment. Don't let customers wonder if you're calling or visiting Thursday.

FIX — When the customer mentioned taking estimates elsewhere, frame the diagnostic process as an Option C callback appointment upfront instead of deferring recommendations to a later call, so they commit before leaving.

FIX — When she couldn't afford the payment plan due to her husband's death, you needed to reconnect with 'What would work for you?' instead of 'wait until it breaks'—that one question in Decision gets you the estimate visit.

FIX — On a maintenance call for an 8-year-old struggling system, pivot to Option C thinking: 'Let me run tests today to see if maintenance fixes this or if an upgrade would better serve you.' Gathers data for a follow-up sales conversation.
FIX — Transcript cuts off before reaching decision phase; unable to assess full call.
FIX — Transcript cuts off before close/flip decision; call not completed for assessment.

FIX — You presented the refrigerant leak damage vividly but ended with 'I can get them out here for an estimate'—use that opening to ask 'Would you like to move forward with getting that specialist estimate this week?' to create urgency.
FIX — Despite excellent nerd work explaining the system issues, you didn't clearly ask the customer to commit to next steps—end with 'Should we schedule the specialist visit this week or next?'

FIX — You did excellent work breaking down the compressor overload issue with amp readings, but ended without a clear call-to-action—'Let's get you scheduled with our comfort specialist to explore your best options—can we do Thursday?'
FIX — When the customer expressed time constraints, ask a discovery question about system comfort or age instead of just reassuring them—that opens the door to Option C.

WIN — When the customer hesitated about joining the membership today, you offered timing flexibility ('you can sign up in winter') then locked in value with specifics ('save 15% on repairs, get an extra year warranty'), which converted the objection into a yes.

FIX — Joe showed genuine empathy about the customer's budget constraints but didn't ask if they'd want replacement cost information after the inspection. When Joe wraps up, he should ask: 'Would you like me to run numbers on what a replacement would cost so you can compare it to the repair cycle you've been in?' This opens a TGL conversation without pressuring today.

FIX — You diagnosed the condenser coil freeze-up and recommended a specialist visit, but didn't ask for a specific time commitment; close with 'Can we get someone out to you Thursday or Friday this week?'

FIX — You asked great questions about comfort zones and history, but stopped after diagnosis without offering options—say 'We could do a blower clean, or I can get our specialist to look at efficiency upgrades.'
FIX — Excellent system explanation and check-in throughout, but you didn't ask for the close—end with 'Should we move forward with the specialist estimate this week?'

FIX — You confirmed the thermostat issue and power settings but stopped short of explaining what's wrong or recommending next steps; say 'The thermostat is stuck—we can either replace it today or I can set up a specialist to look at your full system.'

FIX — You diagnosed the refrigerant leak well and recommended a specialist visit, but didn't present options or ask 'Would you like us to get them scheduled for this week?'—close the loop before you leave.
FIX — This is a very short call with minimal conversation—don't skip the basics even on quick visits; ask at least one question about their concern and mention next steps before you leave.

WIN — You built excellent rapport during diagnosis and clearly explained the compressor failure risk, then asked directly 'Should we go ahead with the replacement?' and customer agreed—the confident nerd work earned the flip.

WIN — When the customer hesitated on system replacement due to timing, you reframed aging-system repairs from 'throw money out the window' to 'explore replacement before $8,600+ failure' and coordinated scheduling with your manager—this moved their objection into a specialist consultation TGL.

WIN — When the customer pushed back on the $2000 upfront cost, you didn't fold—you said 'I can set someone up so that they can give you that information and come and talk to you about it,' turning their concerns into a Thursday TGL by offering comparison shopping instead of a hard sell.

WIN — When customer expressed concern about being without AC for 5 days and frustration with the prior contractor, Joe's detailed technical explanation—showing the dead capacitor (9.82 vs. 45 µF), the humidifier dust buildup, and the cascading compressor failure—built such credibility that when he promised written solutions, the customer flipped to a TGL.
WIN — Navigated tenant-landlord approval gap by clarifying upfront that property manager sign-off was required and committing to follow-up with specific solutions.
WIN — Successfully transitioned customer to next step

FIX — When customer mentioned the bedroom AC staying at 80 degrees and not cooling down properly, that was an opening to present an Option C for a detailed diagnostic rather than just note it and move on to maintenance-only.
WIN — Converted customer frustration about prior plumbing service into trust by validating concerns and committing to escalate feedback to management.
WIN — Your detailed thermal imaging explanation and heart-of-the-system metaphor for the compressor showed exactly why replacement was urgent—the visceral understanding sealed the upgrade agreement.
FIX — When customer mentioned exploring Weldy's AC company, respond with an empathy question about what matters most in deciding between options instead of listing advantages.
FIX — Accepted customer deferral to run equipment to failure without framing control board burnout risk as fire hazard during peak heat demand season.
